items.readable_text:
Content:
If we know a root of a polynomial, we can immediately determine a factor of the polynomial using the factor theorem.

Content:
The factor theorem states that if [MATH: p(x)] is a polynomial and [MATH: x={\color{blue}{r}}] is a root of [MATH: p(x),] meaning that

Content:
[MATH: p({\color{blue}{r}})=0]

Content:
then [MATH: (x-{\color{blue}{r}})] is a factor of [MATH: p(x).]

Content:
The converse of the factor theorem is also true. In other words, if [MATH: (x-{\color{blue}{r}})] is a factor of [MATH: p(x),] then [MATH: x={\color{blue}{r}}] is a root of the polynomial.

Content:
For example, consider the polynomial [MATH: p(x),] defined as

Content:
[MATH: p(x)=x^3-2x^2-x+2.]

Content:
Note that [MATH: x = {\color{blue}2}] is a root of this polynomial:

Content:
[MATH: p(2)|= 2^{3} − 2(2)^{2} − 2 + 2; = 8 − 8 − 2 + 2; = 0]

Content:
Therefore, according to the factor theorem, [MATH: (x-{\color{blue}2})] is a factor of the polynomial. Indeed, it can be shown that this polynomial can be factored as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x^{3} − 2x^{2} − x + 2|= (x − 2)(x^{2} − 1)]

Content:
We'll learn more about factoring polynomials using the factor theorem in future lessons. But for now, we can check that this is correct by multiplying the parentheses.

sections.normalized_html: Determine if [MATH: x+3] is a factor of [MATH: p(x)=x^3+3x^2-3x-9.]
sections.readable_text: Determine if [MATH: x+3] is a factor of [MATH: p(x)=x^3+3x^2-3x-9.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
According to the factor theorem, [MATH: (x-r)] is a factor of [MATH: p(x)] if the root [MATH: x = r] is also a root of [MATH: p(x).]

Here, we are considering [MATH: (x+3).] The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to [MATH: 0] and solving:

[MATH: x + 3|= 0; x|= − 3]

According to the factor theorem, then, [MATH: (x+3)] is a factor of [MATH: p(x)] if the root [MATH: x = -3] is a root of [MATH: p(x).]

So, we just need to check if [MATH: x=-3] is a root of [MATH: p(x).] In other words, we need to check if [MATH: p(-3)=0\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: p(− 3)|= (− 3)^{3} + 3(− 3)^{2} − 3(− 3) − 9; = − 27 + 27 + 9 − 9; = 0]

Indeed, [MATH: p(-3)=0,] so [MATH: x = -3] is a root of the polynomial. Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that [MATH: (x+3)] is indeed a factor of [MATH: p(x).]

According to the factor theorem, [MATH: (ax-b)] is a factor of [MATH: p(x)] if the root [MATH: x = \dfrac{b}{a}] is also a root of [MATH: p(x).]

Here, we are considering [MATH: (4-3x).] The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to [MATH: 0] and solving:

[MATH: 4 − 3x|= 0; 4|= 3x; x|= (4)/(3)]

So, we just need to check if [MATH: x=\dfrac{4}{3}] is a root of [MATH: p(x).] In other words, we need to check if [MATH: p\left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right) =0\mathbin{:}]

Item 3 — Example: Applying the Factor Theorem

Example Prompt:
Determine if [MATH: x+3] is a factor of [MATH: p(x)=x^3+3x^2-3x-9.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
According to the factor theorem, [MATH: (x-r)] is a factor of [MATH: p(x)] if the root [MATH: x = r] is also a root of [MATH: p(x).]

Here, we are considering [MATH: (x+3).] The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to [MATH: 0] and solving:

[MATH: x + 3|= 0; x|= − 3]

According to the factor theorem, then, [MATH: (x+3)] is a factor of [MATH: p(x)] if the root [MATH: x = -3] is a root of [MATH: p(x).]

So, we just need to check if [MATH: x=-3] is a root of [MATH: p(x).] In other words, we need to check if [MATH: p(-3)=0\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: p(− 3)|= (− 3)^{3} + 3(− 3)^{2} − 3(− 3) − 9; = − 27 + 27 + 9 − 9; = 0]

Indeed, [MATH: p(-3)=0,] so [MATH: x = -3] is a root of the polynomial. Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that [MATH: (x+3)] is indeed a factor of [MATH: p(x).]

Item 7 — Example: Applying the Factor Theorem to Factors With Leading Coefficients

Example Prompt:
Determine if [MATH: (4-3x)] is a factor of [MATH: p(x)=-6x^2+11x-4.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
According to the factor theorem, [MATH: (ax-b)] is a factor of [MATH: p(x)] if the root [MATH: x = \dfrac{b}{a}] is also a root of [MATH: p(x).]

Here, we are considering [MATH: (4-3x).] The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to [MATH: 0] and solving:

[MATH: 4 − 3x|= 0; 4|= 3x; x|= (4)/(3)]

According to the factor theorem, then, [MATH: (4-3x)] is a factor of [MATH: p(x)] if the root [MATH: x=\dfrac{4}{3}] is also a root of [MATH: p(x).]

So, we just need to check if [MATH: x=\dfrac{4}{3}] is a root of [MATH: p(x).] In other words, we need to check if [MATH: p\left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right) =0\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: p((4)/(3))|= − 6((4)/(3))^{2} + 11((4)/(3)) − 4; = − 6 ⋅ (16)/(9) + (44)/(3) − 4; = (− 32 + 44 − 12)/(3); = 0]

Indeed, [MATH: p \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right)=0,] so [MATH: x=\dfrac{4}{3}] is a root of the polynomial. Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that [MATH: (4-3x)] is indeed a factor of [MATH: p(x).]
